en: Catuṣpariṣatsūtra (1st),

Section E: The Blessed One, the Bodhisattva, while dwelling at Uruvilvā on the bank of the river Nairañjanā at the foot of the Bodhi tree, was constant in practice, prudent, and devoted to the yoga of cultivation regarding the factors conducive to awakening.
He dwells devotedly.

During the first watch of the night, he directs his mind toward the supernormal knowledge that realizes the domain of psychic power (*ṛddhiviṣayajñānasākṣīkriyābhijñā*), and he experiences various kinds of psychic power. That is to say: having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one; he appears and he disappears.

He experiences this through knowledge and vision: he passes unhindered through walls, through mountains, and through ramparts with his body, just as if through space; he performs the act of diving and surfacing in the earth, just as in water;
he walks on water with his body unhindered, just as on earth; and he travels cross-legged through the sky.
"Just as a winged bird, even these two— the moon and the sun— so powerful and so majestic, he strokes and rubs with his hand,
and even as far as the Brahma-world, he exercises mastery over them with his body.
Thus the Blessed One, the Bodhisattva, while dwelling at Uruvilvā on the bank of the Nairañjanā river at the foot of the Bodhi tree, practiced with constant perseverance.

Being discerning and dwelling devoted to the practice of cultivation regarding the factors conducive to awakening, he experienced various kinds of supernormal powers during the first watch of the night.
Then the Blessed One, the Bodhisattva, while dwelling at Uruvilvā— as previously described— dwelt devotedly [to the practice].

During the first watch of the night, he directed his mind toward the supernormal knowledge that realizes the recollection of past lives. He recollected his manifold past existences; that is to say, one birth, two, three, four, and even many eons of world-dissolution and evolution.
Thus the Blessed One, the Bodhisattva, while dwelling at Uruvilvā on the bank of the Nairañjanā river at the foot of the Bodhi tree, practiced with constant diligence.
Being discerning and dwelling devoted to the practice of cultivation regarding the factors conducive to awakening, he recollects his former births during the first watch of the night.
Then the Blessed One, the Bodhisattva, while dwelling at Uruvilvā— as previously described— dwelt devoted to that practice.
During the middle watch of the night, he directed his mind toward the supernormal knowledge that realizes the power of the divine ear.
With the purified divine ear, which surpasses that of humans, he heard both kinds of sounds— human and non-human— whether they were far or near.

Thus the Blessed One, the Bodhisattva, while dwelling at Uruvilvā on the bank of the river Nairañjanā at the foot of the Bodhi tree— practicing with constancy, prudent, and devoted to the application of cultivation regarding the factors conducive to awakening— experienced the knowledge of the divine ear during the middle watch of the night.
Then the Blessed One, the Bodhisattva, while dwelling at Uruvilvā—as previously described—remained devotedly engaged [in meditation].
During the middle watch of the night, he directed his mind toward the knowledge that realizes the divine eye.
With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he beheld beings passing away and being reborn.
He understands, as they truly are, beings who are beautiful or ugly, lowly or exalted, and those going to a good destination or a bad destination,
according to their karma: "These worthy beings, endowed with misconduct of body, and endowed with misconduct of speech and mind..."

Those who revile the noble ones, who hold wrong views, and who, because of their undertaking of actions and dharmas based on wrong views, for that cause and that condition, at the breaking up of the body after death, are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a state of ruin,
in the hells; or, again, these beings, friends, are endowed with good conduct of body, and endowed with good conduct of speech and mind.

Not reviling the noble ones, possessing right view, and because of undertaking the dharma of actions consistent with right view— for that cause and for that condition— they are, upon the dissolution of the body, reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world, among the gods. Thus the Blessed One, the Bodhisattva, while dwelling at Uruvilvā on the bank of the river Nairañjanā at the foot of the Bodhi tree, practiced with constant diligence.
Being discerning and dwelling devoted to the practice of cultivation regarding the factors conducive to awakening, he experienced the knowledge of the divine eye during the middle watch of the night.
Then the Blessed One, the Bodhisattva, while dwelling at Uruvilvā— as previously described— dwelt devotedly [to that practice].
During the last watch of the night, he directs his mind toward the higher knowledge that realizes the penetration of the minds of others.

He understands, as they truly are, the thoughts and reflections, the mental states and mental objects, of other beings and other individuals. He understands, as it truly is, a mind affected by passion as a mind affected by passion; he understands a mind free from passion as a mind free from passion.

He understands as it really is: a mind with hatred as "a mind with hatred," a mind free from hatred as "free from hatred"; a mind with delusion as "with delusion," a mind free from delusion as "free from delusion"; a distracted mind as "distracted," a concentrated mind as "concentrated"; a sunken mind as "sunken," an uplifted mind as "uplifted"; an agitated mind as "agitated," an unagitated mind as "unagitated"; an unpeaceful mind as "unpeaceful," a peaceful mind as "peaceful"; an unconcentrated mind as "unconcentrated," a concentrated mind as "concentrated"; an uncultivated mind as "uncultivated," a cultivated mind as "cultivated"; and an unliberated mind as "an unliberated mind. Thus he understands as it really is.
He understands, as it truly is, "the mind is liberated; the mind is liberated.

Thus the Bodhisattva, the Blessed One, while dwelling at Uruvilvā on the bank of the river Nairañjanā at the foot of the Bodhi tree—practicing with constancy, prudent, and devoted to the application of cultivation regarding the factors conducive to awakening—during the last watch of the night, dwelt [in this manner].
He experiences the knowledge of the minds of others.
Then the Blessed One, the Bodhisattva, while dwelling at Uruvilvā—as previously described—remained devoted to his practice.
In the final watch of the night, he directed his mind toward the higher knowledge that realizes the destruction of the outflows.

He understands, as it truly is: "This is the noble truth of suffering"; "this is the origin of suffering"; "this is the cessation of suffering"; and "this is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering. For him who thus knows and thus sees, the mind is liberated from the influx of sensual desire, from the influx of existence, and from the influx of ignorance.

He is liberated. In one who is liberated, there arises the knowledge and vision: "I am liberated. "Birth is exhausted for me; the holy life has been lived; what was to be done has been accomplished; I know no further state of existence beyond this.

Thus the Blessed One, while dwelling at Uruvilvā on the bank of the Nairañjanā River at the foot of the Bodhi tree, having accomplished his task and fulfilled his purpose, entered the fire-element as a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Section 1.
Then, it occurred to two deities belonging to the Brahma-realm:
"This Buddha, the Blessed One, is staying at Uruvilvā on the bank of the river Nairañjanā at the foot of the Bodhi tree, having recently attained full awakening."
"Having attained the fire-element, he passes seven days in a single cross-legged posture, and no one offers him almsfood. What if we were to go to him and each praise him individually with verses?
Then two deities from the Brahma-realm, just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm, [vanished from the Brahma-realm and appeared before the Blessed One].
Or as one might extend what has been contracted, even so two deities of the Brahma-realm, having vanished from the Brahma-world, reappeared before the Blessed One.
Then a certain deity of the Brahma-realm spoke this verse:
"Arise, O conqueror in battle! Travel through the world, O caravan leader free from affliction!"
O Sugata, teach the sublime Dharma;
there will be those who shall come to know the jewel of the Dharma. 1.
At that time, a second deity from the Brahmakāyika realm spoke this verse:
"Arise, O victor in battle! Wander through the world, O one who has fulfilled his purpose and is free from affliction!"
For your mind is perfectly pure, like the full moon on the fifteenth day. 2.
Having spoken thus, the two deities of the Brahma-realm vanished on the spot.
Then, after they had departed, the Blessed One arose from that concentration and at that time spoke these verses:
"And whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world..."
And even that heavenly happiness is not worth a sixteenth part of the bliss that comes from the exhaustion of craving. 1.165.1//
Having laid down the heavy burden, one should not take up another;
the taking up of a burden is suffering.
The laying down of the burden is happiness. 2.
Having abandoned all craving,
through the destruction of all conditioned formations and the full understanding of all acquisitions.
They do not come again to renewed existence.

Section 2.1: Experiencing the joy and bliss of liberation, the Buddha, the Blessed One, spent seven days in a single cross-legged posture; he was not offered any alms-food by anyone. Section 2.2: At that time, two merchants, Tripusa and Bhallika, were traveling along that very same road together with about five hundred carts.
Then, it occurred to a certain deity who was formerly a friend, minister, kinsman, or blood relative of the two merchants Triṣaṅku and Bhallika:

"This Buddha, the Blessed One, is dwelling at Uruvilvā on the bank of the river Nairañjanā at the foot of the Bodhi tree; having recently attained full enlightenment, he is experiencing the joy and bliss of liberation. The Buddha, the Blessed One, has spent seven days in a single cross-legged posture."

"He has not been provided with almsfood by anyone. Let the two merchants, Tripusa and Bhallika, be the first to provide him with almsfood; that would be for the long-term welfare, benefit, and happiness of the merchants Tripusa and Bhallika. What if I myself were to take up the initiative for the purpose of providing him with almsfood?"
Then that deity, having pervaded the entire caravan with a sublime radiance, spoke these words to the two merchants, Tripusa and Bhallika:
"Merchants, merchants! This Buddha, the Blessed One, is staying at Urubilvā on the bank of the river Nairañjanā at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
Having recently attained full awakening, he is experiencing the joy and bliss of liberation. For seven days, the Buddha, the Blessed One..."

"He passes the time in a single cross-legged posture; he has not been provided with even a morsel of almsfood by anyone. You two should be the first to provide him with almsfood; that will lead to your welfare, benefit, and happiness for a long time.
Then this thought occurred to the merchants Trapusa and Bhallika: "Surely the Buddha is no ordinary person; surely [he is] no inferior one."

"The teaching of the Dharma, for which even the deities now feel a sense of eager longing, on account of the offering of almsfood to that Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha. Having understood this, they took a great quantity of honey and parched grain flour and approached the place where the Blessed One was.

Having approached and bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, the two merchants Tripuṣa and Bhallika stood to one side. Standing to one side, the two merchants Tripuṣa and Bhallika said this to him: “Venerable sir, we have brought almsfood for the Blessed One, as well as plenty of honey and parched grain flour, intended specifically for the Blessed One. May the Blessed One accept it out of compassion. Then this thought occurred to the Blessed One: “It would not be fitting for me to accept the almsfood with my hand.”
"Just as that non-Buddhist ascetic [thought]: 'What if I were to reflect upon where alms-food was accepted by the former Perfectly Awakened Ones for the benefit of living beings?
The deities informed the Blessed One: 'Venerable Sir, in a bowl, alms-food was accepted by the former Perfectly Awakened Ones.'"

"It has been accepted for the benefit of living beings. Then, the Blessed One, having applied his knowledge and vision, perceived that the alms-food had been accepted in the bowl by previous Perfectly Awakened Ones for the benefit of living beings. Thereupon, the need for a bowl arose for the Blessed One.
Section 3.
Then the four Great Kings, perceiving that a need for a bowl had arisen for the Blessed One, [took] from a certain rocky mountain four stone bowls, unmade by humans and finished by non-humans.
Taking clear, pure, and odorless [garments], they approached the place where the Blessed One was. Having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the four Great Kings said this to the Blessed One:

"Venerable Sir, having understood that a need for a bowl had arisen for the Blessed One, we went to a certain rocky mountain and brought back four stone bowls— unmade by humans, finished by no human hands, transparent, pure, and free from odor. May the Blessed One accept here the alms-food of the merchants Tripiṭaka and Bhallika for the welfare of living beings."

Then this occurred to the Blessed One: "If I accept the bowl of only one great king, there will be dissatisfaction for the other three. If I accept the bowls of two or three, there will be dissatisfaction for the remaining two or one. What if I were to accept the bowls of the four great kings and resolve them into a single bowl?"

Then the Blessed One, having accepted the bowls of the four Great Kings, resolved them into a single bowl. There, the Blessed One accepted the alms-food from the two merchants, Tripusa and Bhallika, for the welfare of living beings.
Then the Blessed One addressed the two merchants, Tripusa and Bhallika: "Come, you two merchants, [approach] the Buddha."
"Go for refuge to the Dharma; go for refuge to that which will be known as the Saṅgha in the future time—go for refuge to that as well.
"Venerable Sir, we two go for refuge to the Buddha; we go for refuge to the Dharma; we two also go for refuge to that which will be known as the Saṅgha in the future time."
"Let us go.
Then the Blessed One expressed his approval of that gift of the merchants Tripuṣa and Bhallika with this expression of appreciation:
"The ripening of meritorious deeds is blissful."
His intention is fulfilled,
and he swiftly attains supreme peace and liberation.
Whatever adversities come from others— whether from deities or from the hosts of Māra— they are unable to create an obstacle.
Indeed, for the one who has performed meritorious deeds, [it belongs] to the doer.
For if he exerts himself with noble wisdom and is possessed of renunciation,
it is indeed for the sake of making an end to suffering.
There is comfort for one who sees clearly. 3.
Then the two merchants, Tripuṣa and Bhallika, having rejoiced and delighted in the words of the Blessed One, bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and departed from his presence.
Then the Blessed One, having received almsfood from the two merchants Tripuṣa and Bhallika, performed his meal in a certain place.
In that place, even the honey was wind-disorder-inducing, and even the churned drinks were wind-disorder-inducing; consequently, a sickness of wind-disorder arose in the Blessed One.
Then Māra, the Evil One, perceiving that the Blessed One was suffering from a sickness of wind-disorder, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
"Pass away, Blessed One! The time for the Parinirvāṇa of the Sugata has arrived."
Wal_4.5 Only in the parallels Wal_4.6:
"Evil One, I shall not enter final nirvana until my disciples have become wise, discerning, and intelligent;
until they are capable of refuting, in accordance with the Dharma, any opposing disputants as they arise, and are capable of establishing their own doctrine."
"The monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen will be purified; my holy life will become widespread, extensive, and well-proclaimed among gods and humans.
Then, it occurred to Māra the Evil One: "The ascetic Gautama is about to attain final nirvana. Realizing this, he became sorrowful, dejected, and full of regret, and vanished right there.
Section 5.
Wal_5.1 Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, perceiving that the Blessed One had fallen ill with a wind-disorder,
[went] from a great grove of *harītakī* trees not far from the jambu tree after which Jambudvīpa is named, [and brought] *harītakī* fruits from there.
Endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and flavor, he took them and approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One: "Here, O Venerable Blessed One, [I have taken these fruits] for the Blessed One."

"Perceiving that a wind-related illness had arisen, I have brought from a great grove of *harītakī* trees—not far from the rose-apple tree (*jambu*) after which Jambudvīpa is named—*harītakī* fruits endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and taste. May the Blessed One consume them;
once consumed by the Blessed One, they will regulate the wind and pacify this wind-related illness."

When the Blessed One had eaten them, they harmonized his wind and allayed the illness caused by the wind disorder; consequently, it became more bearable and more sustainable for the Blessed One. Section 6.

Then the Blessed One, having stayed at the foot of the Bodhi tree for as long as he pleased, went to the abode of Mucalinda, the king of the nāgas. Having arrived, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
At that time, a seven-day unseasonable cloud arrived at the abode of Mucalinda, the king of the nāgas.

Then, the nāga king Mucalinda, perceiving that a seven-day unseasonable cloud had arrived, emerged from his abode, coiled his body around [the Blessed One] seven times, and stood with a great hood spread over him, thinking: "May no harm come to the Blessed One."
"For these seven days it will be cold; may there be no heat, and may the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping reptiles not torment the body.
Then the Naga king Mucalinda, perceiving that the seven-day unseasonal cloud had passed away, [approached] the Blessed One’s body.

Having unwrapped his body and become adorned with armlets, earrings, variegated garlands, ornaments, and ointments, he extended his joined palms toward where the Blessed One was and addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"May this seven-day period not be cold for the Blessed One, nor hot; may the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping reptiles not cause affliction to your body."
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Seclusion is bliss for one who is content, who has heard the Dharma, and who sees."
In this world, the happiness that cannot be destroyed consists in restraint toward all living beings. 1.//
Blissful is the fading away of passion in the world,
the transcendence of sensual desires,
and the subduing of the conceit "I am."
This indeed is the supreme happiness. 2.// //
Section 7.1 Then the Blessed One, having stayed as long as he pleased in the abode of the nāga king Mucalinda, approached the foot of the Bodhi tree. 7.2 Having arrived,
he sat down upon the prepared grass mat, assuming the cross-legged posture, holding his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
Having established mindfulness before him, he spent seven days in a single cross-legged posture, contemplating this very twelvefold dependent origination in both forward and reverse order:
namely, "when this exists, that comes to be; from the arising of this, that arises," that is to say, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise.
With volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases;
with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging;
with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; and with birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise.
In this way, there is the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.
That is to say: when this does not exist, that does not come to be; from the cessation of this, that ceases. That is to say:

from the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations; from the cessation of volitional formations, the cessation of consciousness; from the cessation of consciousness, the cessation of name-and-form.

From the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense-bases; from the cessation of the six sense-bases comes the cessation of contact; from the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling; from the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving; from the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging;

from the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence; from the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth; and from the cessation of birth come the cessation of old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
In this way, there is the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.
Then, at the end of those very seven days, the Blessed One arose from that concentration and, at that time, spoke these verses:
"When these phenomena manifest..."
For the ardent brahmin who meditates,
all doubts depart when he understands phenomena together with their causes. 1.
When these phenomena become manifest to the ardent and meditative brahmin,
then all his doubts depart.
When one understands suffering together with its cause.
When these phenomena become manifest to the ardent, meditating brahmin,
then all his doubts vanish away.
When he realizes the exhaustion of sensations. 3. // //
When these phenomena become manifest to the ardent, meditating brahmin,
then all his doubts vanish away.
When he understands the exhaustion of conditions. 4. //
When these phenomena become manifest to the ardent, meditating brahmin,
then all his doubts vanish away.
When he realizes the destruction of the outflows.
When these phenomena become manifest to the ardent, meditating brahmin,
they remain illuminating the entire world.
Just as the sun has risen in the sky.
When these phenomena become manifest to the ardent, meditating brahmin,
he stands dispelling the army of Māra.
For the Buddha is completely liberated from the fetters. 7.
Section 8.1 Then this occurred to the Blessed One:

8.2 "The Dharma realized by me is profound, profound in its appearance, difficult to see, difficult to understand, beyond the sphere of logic, inaccessible to reasoning, subtle, precise, and to be experienced by the wise and the learned."

“If I were to announce this to others and they did not understand it, that would be a weariness for me, a fatigue, and a lack of mental progress. Suppose, then, that I dwell alone in the forest, on a mountain slope, devoted to the practice of dwelling in happiness in the present life.”
Thus, in that situation, the Blessed One’s mind inclined toward dwelling in a state of little concern, rather than toward teaching the Dharma.
Then, this thought occurred to Brahmā, the Lord of the Assembly:
"Alas, this world is perishing! Alas, this world is being destroyed! For now, at this time, the Tathāgatas..."

"Arhats, perfectly awakened ones, arise in the world as rarely as the udumbara flower. And today the mind of this Blessed One inclines toward dwelling in ease, not toward teaching the Dharma. What if I were to go and entreat him?
Then Brahmā, Lord of the Assembly, just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, [vanished from the Brahma-world and appeared before the Blessed One].
Or he might contract [his limbs]; in just this way, Brahmā, the Lord of the Assembly, vanished from the Brahma-world and reappeared before the Blessed One.
Then, at that time, Brahmā, the Lord of the Assembly, spoke this verse:
"In the past, it appeared among the Magadhans..."
For the Dharma is indeed impure, realized with stains;
open the door of the Deathless and speak the Dharma realized as stainless.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke this verse:
“With great difficulty have I attained it;
O Brahmā, the barren wastes have been shattered.”
For this Dharma is not well understood by those who are overwhelmed by craving for existence.
Those stained by passion will not see the path that goes against the stream, which is profound and difficult to perceive.
They are shrouded by a mass of darkness.

“Venerable Sir, there are beings born in the world and grown up in the world who possess sharp faculties, middling faculties, and even dull faculties; who are of good disposition, easy to instruct, possessing little dust, and of a nature with little dust, yet who fall away because they have not heard the Dharma.
May the Blessed One teach the Dharma; may the Sugata teach the Dharma. There will be those who understand the jewel of the Dharma.”
Then it occurred to the Blessed One: "What if I were to survey the world myself with the eye of a Buddha?

The Blessed One, surveying the world himself with the eye of a Buddha, saw that there are beings born in the world and grown up in the world who possess sharp faculties, middling faculties, and dull faculties; who are of good disposition and easy to instruct.

There were those with little dust in their eyes, belonging to a lineage with little dust, who were falling away because they had not heard the Dharma. And upon seeing them, great compassion arose within him toward sentient beings.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke this verse:
I shall open the door to the Deathless;
let those who desire to hear and possess faith rejoice.
I do not speak at length out of a desire to find fault.
O Brahmin, [you have taught] the sublime Dharma among human beings.

Then this thought occurred to Brahmā Sabhāpati: "The Blessed One will teach the Dharma; the Sugata will teach the Dharma. Having understood this, filled with joy, satisfaction, gladness, elation, and a sense of rapture and well-being, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and vanished right there.
Section 9.1 Then this occurred to the Blessed One: "To whom indeed should I first teach the Dharma?
9.2 Then this occurred to the Blessed One: "What if I were to first teach the Dharma to Ārāḍa Kālāma?"
"He who was my very own former teacher, whom I honored with the highest honor and worshiped with the highest worship, and in whom I found supreme confidence and satisfaction.
The deities informed the Blessed One: "Ārāḍa Kālāma has been dead for seven days."

The Blessed One also applied his knowledge and vision, and it occurred to him: “Ārāḍa Kālāma has been dead for seven days. Then this thought arose in the Blessed One: “Alas, what a great loss is this death of Ārāḍa! For he did not hear this Dharma and Vinaya;
had he heard this Dharma and Vinaya, he would have understood this Dharma and Vinaya.”

Then this thought occurred to the Blessed One: "To whom, indeed, should I first teach the Dharma? Then this thought occurred to the Blessed One: "What if I were to first teach the Dharma to Udraka Rāmaputra, who was my former teacher and who honored me with the highest honor and worshipped me with the highest worship among the supreme [beings]?"
And he became pleased with and satisfied by the conditions.

The deities informed the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, Udraka Rāmaputra has passed away during the night. Then, as the Blessed One directed his attention, his knowledge and vision arose: "Udraka Rāmaputra has passed away during the night."

Then this occurred to the Blessed One: "Alas, what a great loss for Udraka Rāmaputra at the time of his death, that he did not hear this Dharma and Vinaya! Had he heard this Dharma and Vinaya, he would have understood this Dharma and Vinaya."

Then this occurred to the Blessed One: "To whom, indeed, should I first teach the Dharma? Then this occurred to the Blessed One: "What if I were to first teach the Dharma to the group of five monks, who formerly attended upon me with reverence and affection while I dwelt devoted to the practice of the abandonment of suffering?"

Then this occurred to the Blessed One: "Where indeed are the group of five monks staying now? With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the Blessed One saw that the group of five monks were staying at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana.

Having stayed at the foot of the Bodhi tree as long as he pleased, he set out on a journey toward Bārāṇasī, the city of the Kāśīs. At that time, Upaga the Ājīvika was traveling along that very same road. From afar, Upaga the Ājīvika saw the Blessed One. Having seen him...
And he spoke further as follows:

"Venerable Gautama, your faculties are serene; your facial complexion is pure and the color of your skin is bright. Who, venerable Gautama, is your teacher? With reference to whom have you gone forth? Or whose Dharma do you find pleasing?"
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
“I have no teacher; there is no one equal to me to be found.”
I am the one perfectly awakened one in the world,
having attained supreme enlightenment.
I am the conqueror of all, the knower of all in this world, and I am unsullied by any phenomena whatsoever; having abandoned everything, free from craving, I am liberated.
Having realized it for myself, whom indeed should I point to as my teacher?
Whom should I point to as my teacher? For I am peerless and incomparable;
having myself attained awakening, I am the Tathāgata, the teacher of gods and humans.
He is omniscient and endowed with the powers of an omniscient one.
I am the Arhat in the worlds;
I am the unsurpassed one in the worlds, including those with their gods.
I am the Victor, the conqueror of Māra.
"Venerable Gautama," he said, "you call yourself a 'Conqueror' (jina). Indeed,
those like me who have attained the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣaya) should be known as Conquerors."
“Evil states have been conquered by me;
therefore, I am indeed a Jina.
“Where will you go, venerable Gautama? Wal_10.9
I shall go to Vārāṇasī to beat the drum of the Dharma and to set in motion the wheel of the Dharma.
That which has not been set in motion in the worlds.
For the virtuous do not manifest themselves once they have understood the turning of the world;
for the Buddhas are eternally at peace.
"O Venerable Gautama, you say that the Conqueror has crossed over the attachment to the world. Having said this, Upaga the Ājīvaka departed from the path.
Section 11.
Then the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the country of Kāśi, arrived at Vārāṇasī. At that time, the group of five monks were staying at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana.
The group of five monks saw the Blessed One from afar; having seen him, they stepped aside from one another and made an agreement among themselves.

"Sirs, here comes that ascetic Gautama— slack, luxurious, and living in abundance; having strayed from his exertion, he now partakes of substantial food, namely boiled rice and sour gruel, he anoints his limbs with ghee and oil, and he bathes his body with warm water."

When he has approached us, he is not to be greeted, nor is he to be saluted; we are not to rise and invite him to take a seat, but rather, having already prepared seats, he is to be addressed thus: "Venerable Gautama, there are seats available; if you wish, please sit down."

In whatever manner the Blessed One approached to see the group of five monks, in that same manner the five monks, unable to endure the Blessed One’s splendor, majesty, and dignity, rose from their seats; some prepared a seat for the Blessed One, some set out water for washing the feet and a footstool to one side, and some [prepared] robes.
They accepted [the invitation] and said, "May the venerable Gautama sit on the seat that has been prepared.
Then it occurred to the Blessed One: "Alas, these deluded men have fallen away from their own agreement. Having understood this, he sat down on the very seat that had been prepared.
At that time, the group of five monks addressed the Blessed One excessively with his name, with his clan name, and with the address "Venerable Sir."
There, the Blessed One addressed the group of five monks: "Monks, do not address the Tathāgata by name, nor by his clan, nor by the title 'Venerable.

For what reason? Monks, whatever person addresses the Tathāgata excessively by name, by clan, or by the title 'Venerable,' that leads to the long-term misfortune, harm, and suffering of that deluded man."

They said this: "Venerable Gautama, by means of that former deportment, conduct, and practice of austerities, you did not attain anything superior to human conditions—a noble distinction, realization, knowledge, vision, or a state of abiding in comfort. How much less so now, when you have become lax, indulgent in luxuries, and live a life of abundance?"
“Deluded regarding abandonment, you now consume coarse food—rice and boiled beans—and you anoint your limbs with ghee and oil, and bathe your body with warm water.
Then the Blessed One said this to the group of five monks: “Do you not see, monks, how the Tathāgata’s face is now different from before, and how his faculties are serene?”
Or [is there] a distinction?
"Yes, indeed, O Gautama.
"Monks, these two extremes should not be pursued, should not be cultivated, and should not be attended by one who has gone forth."

"That which is devotion to the pleasure of sensual desires— low, vulgar, common, and belonging to ordinary people— and that which is devotion to self-mortification— painful, ignoble, and unproductive"— not approaching either of these two extremes, there is a middle way that produces vision, produces knowledge, leads to peace, conduces to tranquility, and results in direct knowledge, awakening, and [nirvana].

It leads to Nirvāṇa. What is the middle way? It is the noble eightfold path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration as the eighth.

The Blessed One was able to instruct the group of five monks with this method of instruction: the Blessed One would instruct two of the group of five monks before the morning meal, while three would enter the village for alms; whatever the group of three obtained, that would sustain the group of six.

And the Blessed One would instruct three of the group of five monks after the meal, while two would enter the village for alms; with what the pair brought back, the group of five was sustained, as the Tathāgata himself ate only at the proper time.

There, the Blessed One addressed the group of five monks: "Monks, regarding these things unheard of before, as I applied my mind thoroughly, the eye arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, and insight arose: ‘This is the noble truth of suffering. Monks, regarding these things unheard of before, as I applied my mind thoroughly, the eye arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, and insight arose:
‘This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering; this is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering; this is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’"
"Thus, monks, as I applied my mind thoroughly to these things unheard of before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, and awakening arose.
'That noble truth of suffering, having been directly known, must be fully understood'— thus, monks, as I applied my mind thoroughly to these things unheard of before, vision arose."

"Knowledge, vision, and awakening arose. Monks, regarding that noble truth of the origin of suffering as something to be abandoned through direct knowledge— when I applied systematic attention to these teachings unheard of before,
vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, and awakening arose."

"Monks, regarding that noble truth of the cessation of suffering which is to be realized through direct knowledge: as I applied my mind thoroughly to these teachings unheard of before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, and awakening arose.
Regarding that noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering which is to be developed through direct knowledge: as I..."
“Monks, as I applied my mind thoroughly to things unheard of before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, and awakening arose.
‘That noble truth of suffering has been fully understood through direct knowledge’— monks, as I applied my mind thoroughly to things unheard of before, vision arose.”

Knowledge, vision, wisdom, and awakening arose. Monks, regarding that noble truth of the origin of suffering, [the thought] "it has been abandoned through direct knowledge" arose in me—among dharmas unheard of before—as I attended to them with wise reflection;
vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, and awakening arose.
"Monks, regarding that noble truth of the cessation of suffering, it was realized through direct higher knowledge by me when I applied systematic attention to things unheard of before;
thus, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, and awakening arose.
Monks, regarding that noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering, it was cultivated through direct higher knowledge by me..."

“Monks, as I applied my mind thoroughly to these dharmas unheard of before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, and awakening arose. Monks, as long as this threefold revolution and twelvefold aspect regarding these four noble truths had not yet produced vision, knowledge, wisdom, and awakening in me, for that long, monks, I did not [claim full enlightenment] from this world.”

“Monks, as long as I did not dwell extensively with a mind free from perversion— liberated, escaped, detached, and completely released from the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, and from this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans— I did not claim to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.”

Monks, when for me regarding these four noble truths this vision arose in its three rounds and twelve aspects— when knowledge, science, and awakening arose— then I was liberated from this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, from this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans; I was released, emerged, detached, and utterly freed.
I dwelt frequently with a mind free from perversion; therefore, monks, I knew: "I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Section 13.
While this discourse on the Dharma was being spoken, the dust-free, stainless eye of Dharma regarding all phenomena arose in the Venerable Kauṇḍinya and in eighty thousand deities.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Kauṇḍinya:
"Kauṇḍinya, have you understood the Dharma?"
“It has been understood, Blessed One. “Kauṇḍinya, have you understood the Dharma? “It has been understood, Sugata.”
"The Dharma has been understood by the Venerable Kauṇḍinya; therefore, 'Ājñātakauṇḍinya' (He-Who-Has-Understood-Kauṇḍinya) became the designation for the Venerable Kauṇḍinya.
When the Venerable Kauṇḍinya had understood the Dharma, the terrestrial yakṣas raised their voices and proclaimed the sound:
'Friends, this has been taught by the Blessed One at Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana, as the Dharma discourse consisting of three turnings and twelve aspects.'"

"The Wheel of Dharma has been set in motion, which cannot be turned back by any ascetic, brahmin, god, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world in accordance with the Dharma— for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many,
out of compassion for the world, and for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans. Thus, the divine hosts will increase and the asura hosts will diminish."
Having heard the sound of the terrestrial yakṣas, the yakṣas who roam the atmosphere, the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa gods,

the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods— in that very instant, in that very moment, in that very second, and in that very instant-moment-second, the sound reached as far as the Brahma-world.
The gods of the Brahma-realm raised their voices and proclaimed this sound:

"Friends, in Varanasi, at Rishipatana in the Deer Park, the Blessed One has set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dharma— threefold in its revolution and twelvefold in its aspects— which cannot be turned back by any ascetic, brahmin, god, or Mara."

“Whether by Brahmā or by anyone else in the world, it is in accordance with the Dharma that [this wheel] has been turned for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans; thus the divine hosts will increase and the hosts of asuras will diminish.

Thus was the Dharma-wheel—threefold in its revolutions and twelvefold in its aspects—set in motion by the Blessed One at Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana. Therefore, of this Dharma-discourse...
"Setting in motion the wheel of Dharma" is a designation.
In that regard, the Blessed One addressed the group of five monks a second time.
Monks, there are these four noble truths. Which four?
The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
What is the noble truth of suffering?
Birth is suffering; aging is suffering; illness is suffering; death is suffering; separation from the beloved is suffering; association with the unloved is suffering;
not obtaining what one desires and seeks is also suffering. In short, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering. For the full comprehension of this, the Noble Eightfold Path is to be cultivated.
Wal_14.6 What is the noble truth of the origin of suffering?
Wal_14.7 It is craving, which leads to renewed existence, is accompanied by delight and lust, and finds delight here and there; for its abandonment, the noble eightfold path is to be cultivated.
Wal_14.8 What is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering?

The Noble Eightfold Path is to be cultivated for the sake of realizing the complete abandonment, relinquishment, casting off, destruction, fading away, cessation, pacification, and disappearance of this very craving— which leads to renewed existence, is accompanied by delight and passion, and finds delight here and there.
What is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering?
It is the noble eightfold path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration;
this too is to be cultivated.

While this Dharma discourse was being spoken, the mind of the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya was liberated from the outflows through non-clinging; and for the remaining five monks, the dustless, stainless Dharma-eye arose regarding all phenomena.
At that time, there was one Arhat in the world: the Blessed One as the first, and [Ājñātakauṇḍinya] as the second.
In that place, the Blessed One addressed the remaining five monks:
"Monks, form is not-self. Monks, if form were self, form would not lead to affliction and suffering; and one could obtain regarding form: 'Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus.'"
"It was so, monks.
Therefore, because form is not-self, form leads to affliction and suffering, and one cannot obtain regarding form: 'Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus.'"

“Monks, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not-self. Monks, if consciousness were self, consciousness would not lead to affliction, and one could obtain [the wish]: ‘Let my consciousness be thus; let my consciousness not be thus.
But because consciousness is not-self, therefore consciousness leads to affliction and suffering, and one cannot obtain [the wish]: ‘Let my consciousness be thus; let my consciousness not be thus.’”
"So it was.
"What do you think, monks: is form permanent or impermanent? "Impermanent, Venerable Sir.
"And that which is impermanent, is it suffering or not suffering? "Suffering, Venerable Sir."
Furthermore, that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—would a learned noble disciple regard it as a self, thinking, "This is mine, this am I, this is my self"? "No, Venerable Sir.
"In the same way, are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness permanent or impermanent?"
“Impermanent, Venerable Sir.
“But that which is impermanent, is it suffering or not suffering?
“Suffering, Venerable Sir.”
"Furthermore, monks, whatever is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—would a learned noble disciple regard that as a self, thinking: 'This is mine, this am I, this is my self'?
"No, venerable sir.
"Therefore, monks, whatever form there may be—whether past, future, or present; internal or external—"

Whether gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all that is not mine, I am not this, and this is not my self. Thus, this should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom. In the same way, whatever feeling there is, whatever perception there is, whatever formations there are, and whatever consciousness there is—whether past, future, or present—[all that is not mine, I am not this, and this is not my self]. Thus, this should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom.

Whether internal or external, coarse or subtle, inferior or superior, whether far or near—all that is to be seen with right wisdom, exactly as it is: "This is not mine; this I am not; this is not my self."

Monks, when a learned noble disciple does not regard these five aggregates of clinging as self or as belonging to a self, by so regarding them he does not cling to anything in the world. Not clinging, he is not agitated;
being unagitated, he personally attains parinirvāṇa, [knowing]: "Birth is exhausted for me, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done."
"I know no further existence beyond this that needs to be done.

While this discourse on the Dharma was being spoken, the minds of the remaining five monks were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging. At that time, there were five Arhats in the world, and the Blessed One was the sixth.

At that time, in Vārāṇasī, there lived Yaśas, the son of a leading family. Day after day, having played, enjoyed himself, and amused himself with music consisting entirely of women, his body became exhausted and his body slumped forward;
he fell right away into a deep sleep. Those women also, their bodies exhausted, their bodies weary, and their bodies slumped forward, fell right away [into a deep sleep].
They had fallen into a deep sleep.

Yaśas, the son of the head of the guild, having woken from a dream during the night, saw all those women disheveled, naked, with their hair disarrayed and arms flung out, lying there stark naked and babbling.
Upon seeing this, the perception of a cemetery arose within his own inner apartments. Then Yaśas, the son of the head of the guild—

Descending from his great couch and putting on a pair of jeweled sandals worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], he went toward the gate of the inner apartments; having arrived, he let out a cry: "I am beset! I am afflicted! O worthy ones! Thereupon, non-human beings opened the gate for him and caused his voice to vanish.

Then Yaśas, the son of the head of the guild, went to the gate of his residence; having arrived, he cried out in a weak voice, "I am beset! I am afflicted! O worthy ones! Thereupon, non-human beings opened the gate for him and caused his voice to disappear.
Then Yaśas, the son of the head of the guild, went to the city gate; having arrived, he cried out in a weak voice, "I am beset! I am afflicted! O worthy ones! Thereupon, the non-human beings...
They opened the door and made the sound disappear.
Then Yaśas, the son of the head of the guild, went to the bank of the river Bārakā.
At that time, the Blessed One was on the bank of the river Bārakā, outside the monastery, walking back and forth in the open air.

He paced back and forth almost entirely waiting for Yaśas, the son of a preeminent family. Yaśas, the son of a preeminent family, saw the Blessed One from afar; having seen him, he cried out with a loud voice, "I am beset, O Śramaṇa!
I am afflicted, O Śramaṇa!"
Then the Blessed One said this to Yaśas, the son of a prominent family: “Come, young man; here is a place for you that is free from affliction, free from harm.

Then Yaśas, the son of a prominent family, cast aside a pair of jeweled sandals worth a hundred thousand [pieces] on the bank of the river Bārakā, crossed over the river Bārakā, and approached the Blessed One.

Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side. Then the Blessed One, taking Yaśas, the son of a leading family, went to his own monastery. Having arrived, he sat down on the seat prepared for him.
Once seated, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened Yaśas, the son of a leading family, with a discourse on the Dharma.

He inspires and gladdens them with that Dharma discourse concerning the past lives of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones— namely, a discourse on giving, a discourse on morality, and a discourse on heaven; and he extensively elucidates the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding sensual pleasures, as well as the advantages of renunciation and seclusion, and the factors conducive to purification.

When the Blessed One saw that his mind was confident, prepared, joyful, free from hindrances, capable, and competent to understand the preeminent teaching of the Dharma, then he [expounded] that preeminent teaching of the Dharma of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, namely: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path— the Four Noble Truths.

He explained it in detail: "Just as a clean cloth, free from stains and ready for dyeing, takes on the color perfectly when placed in a dye-vat, even so did Yaśas, the son of a leading family, while seated on that very seat, [realize] the four noble truths."
He realized, namely: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

Then Yaśas, the son of the head of the guild, having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, known the Dharma, and plunged deeply into the Dharma, crossed over doubt, transcended uncertainty, became independent of others, and was no longer led by others; he attained fearlessness regarding the teachings in the Teacher’s instruction.
Rising from his seat, draping his upper robe over one shoulder, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, he said this to the Blessed One:

"I have transcended, O Venerable One; I have transcended! I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower from this day forward, for as long as life lasts, as one who has taken refuge."
[The people] had gone and were full of faith.

Thinking, "He must have gone outside," he dispatched horse-messengers to the four directions and himself went toward the river Bārakā together with men holding torches in their hands. There,
the householder of eminent family saw on the bank of the river Bārakā a pair of jeweled sandals worth a hundred thousand pieces that had been cast away.

Then the Blessed One performed such a feat of supernatural power that the householder Agṛkulika saw the youth Yaśas no longer seated on that very seat.
Then the householder Agṛkulika approached the Blessed One; having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:

“Therefore, householder, sit down; it is possible that you may see the youth Yaśas seated right here on this very seat upon his arrival. Then this thought occurred to the householder, the head of the clan: “Surely the Blessed One must have seen the youth Yaśas, for the Blessed One has spoken thus: ‘Therefore, householder, sit down; it is possible that you may see him seated right here…’”

Knowing that he would see the youth Yaśas seated on this very seat, the householder was thrilled, satisfied, joyful, elated, and filled with a sense of gladness and happiness; he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
As the householder of eminent family sat to one side, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dharma.
He inspires and gladdens them with that Dharma discourse which is appropriate for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, to deliver at the time of their passing away;

namely, a discourse on giving, a discourse on ethical conduct, a discourse on heaven; and he extensively elucidates the gratification, the danger, and the defilement and purification regarding sensual pleasures, as well as the benefits of renunciation and seclusion, and the qualities conducive to purification. When [he does so]...

The Blessed One saw that his mind was confident, prepared, joyful, and free from hindrances, and that he was capable and competent to understand the preeminent teaching of the Dharma; then, the Blessed One gave that preeminent teaching of the Dharma of the Buddhas, namely, the four noble truths in detail: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
He elucidated it as follows: "Just as a clean cloth, free from stains and ready for dyeing,
takes on the color perfectly when placed in a dye-vat, even so the householder Agrikulika, seated on that very seat,
realized the four noble truths— namely, suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path."
Then the householder Agrakulika, having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, known the Dharma, and plunged deeply into the Dharma—
having crossed over doubt, transcended uncertainty, becoming independent of others and no longer led by others, having attained fearlessness regarding the teachings in the Teacher’s dispensation—
rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, he addressed the Blessed One as follows:

“I have transcended, O Venerable One; I have transcended! I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. May you accept me as a lay follower from this day forward, for as long as life lasts, one who has gone for refuge with deep faith.”

While this Dharma discourse was being spoken, the dust-free, stainless eye of Dharma arose regarding all phenomena for the householder Agrakulika, and the mind of the youth Yaśas was liberated from the outflows through non-clinging.
Then the Blessed One, having withdrawn those miraculous manifestations, at that time spoke these verses:
Even if one is adorned, let them practice the Dharma— tamed, peaceful, self-controlled, and living a life of celibacy—
having laid aside the rod toward all living beings.
He is a brahmin, he is a śramaṇa, he is a bhikṣu.
Then the householder Agrakulika said this to the youth Yaśas:
"Come, youth, let us go home; your mother, her body exhausted and weary, is lamenting.
Then the Blessed One said this to the householder Agrakulika:

"What do you think, householder? Since one has now realized the four noble truths— suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path— by means of the knowledge of one beyond training and the vision of one beyond training, would such a person ever again live as a householder, dwelling in a home with the enjoyment of stored possessions, or enjoy sensual pleasures?"
“No, Venerable Sir. “Just as you, householder, have realized the four noble truths—

suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path— with the knowledge of one in training and the vision of one in training, even so has Prince Yaśas realized them with the knowledge of one beyond training.”
By means of the vision of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the four noble truths have been realized: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

"It is a gain, O Venerable One, for Prince Yaśas; it is a great gain for him that by means of the knowledge of one beyond training and the vision of one beyond training, the four noble truths have been realized: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path."

“It would be well, Blessed One, if you would approach the foremost family with Prince Yaśas as your attendant monk, out of compassion. The Blessed One consented to the householder of the foremost family by remaining silent.
Then the householder of the foremost family, understanding the Blessed One’s consent through his silence, bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet and departed from the Blessed One’s presence.

At that time, there were six Arhats in the world, and the Blessed One was the seventh. Then, at the end of that very night, the Blessed One, with the Venerable Yaśas as his attendant monk, went to the residence of the householder Agṛakulika.
The two elderly women, the senior wife and the former second wife of the venerable Yaśas, saw the Blessed One from afar.
Upon seeing him, they prepared a seat for the Blessed One and said, "May the Blessed One sit upon this prepared seat. The Blessed One sat down upon the prepared seat.

Then the venerable Yaśas’s mother-in-law and his former wife bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As the venerable Yaśas’s mother-in-law and his former wife were sitting there to one side, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dharma, such as is characteristic of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.

First, he delivers a discourse on the Dharma concerning the timely matters, namely: a discourse on generosity, a discourse on ethical conduct, and a discourse on heaven; he extensively elucidates the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding sensual pleasures, as well as the benefits of renunciation and seclusion, and the factors conducive to purification.

When the Blessed One saw that their minds were confident, prepared, joyful, and free from hindrances, and that they were capable and competent to understand the most excellent teaching of the Dharma, he then fully proclaimed in detail that most excellent teaching of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones— namely, the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

Just as a clean cloth, free from stains and ready for dyeing, would properly take the dye when placed in a dyepot, even so, while seated on that very same seat, the elder wife and the former second wife of the venerable Yaśas realized the four noble truths— namely, suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Then the elder wife and the former second wife of the venerable Yaśas—having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, known the Dharma, and plunged into the Dharma;

having crossed over doubt and transcended uncertainty; having become independent of others and no longer led by others; having attained fearlessness regarding the teachings in the doctrine of the Teacher—rose from their seats, draped their upper robes over one shoulder, and approached the Blessed One.
Having bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One, they said this to him:

"We have come, Venerable Sir; we have come. We both go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. Please accept us as lay followers from this day forward, as long as life lasts, having gone for refuge and being filled with faith."
Then the Blessed One, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the venerable Yaśas’s mother-in-law and his former wife with a discourse on the Dharma,
rose from his seat and departed.
Section 19.

In Vārāṇasī, the second, third, fourth, and fifth sons of the leading families— Pūrṇa, Vimala, Gavāmpati, Subāhu, and Yaśas, the eldest son of the leading family— heard that [the Blessed One] had shaved off his hair and beard, donned saffron robes,
and out of genuine faith gone forth from the home into the homeless state.

Having heard this, it occurred to them: "Surely the Buddha will not be inferior, nor will his teaching of the Dharma be inferior, since now Yaśas, the son of a leading guild-president, who is so delicate and accustomed to comfort, has shaved off his hair and beard, donned saffron robes, and out of genuine faith gone forth from the home to the homeless life. What if...
“May we too, having shaved off our hair and beards and donned saffron robes, go forth from the home into the homeless state with perfect faith.
Then the second, third, fourth, and fifth sons of the clan—Pūrṇa, Vimala, Gavāmpati, and Subāhu—approached the Blessed One; having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One.
Having paid homage, they stood to one side.
Standing to one side, Pūrṇa, Vimala, Gavāmpati, and Subāhu said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, may we receive the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of monks within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya; may we lead the holy life under the Blessed One."

Those venerable ones obtained the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk within this well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya. Having thus gone forth, those venerable ones dwelt alone, secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute.
While dwelling alone, secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute, for the sake of which noble sons [leave the household life]—that goal they realized.

Having shaved off their hair and beard and donned saffron robes, they go forth from the home to the homeless life out of perfect faith. Having realized for themselves through direct knowledge in this very life that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life, they abide therein and declare: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done."
"We know no further existence beyond this.
At that time, there were ten Arhats in the world, with the Blessed One as the eleventh.
Section 20.

In Vārāṇasī, fifty prominent village youths heard that Yaśas, the son of a leading family, along with the second, third, fourth, and fifth sons of leading families— Pūrṇa, Vimala, Gavāmpati, and Subāhu— had shaved off their hair and beards, donned saffron robes,
and out of genuine faith gone forth from the home to the homeless life.
Having heard this, it occurred to them: "Surely the Buddha is not inferior, nor is his proclamation of the Dharma inferior,
since Yaśas, Pūrṇa, Vimala, Gavāmpati, Subāhu, and likewise those who were delicate and seekers of pleasure,
have now shaved off their hair and beards, donned saffron robes, and out of genuine faith gone forth from the home to the homeless life."
Having heard this, they approached the Blessed One; having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the fifty village boys, who were exceedingly well-favored, said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable Sir, may we receive the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of monks in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya? May we lead the holy life under the Blessed One.”

Those venerable ones obtained the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk within this well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya. Having thus gone forth, those venerable ones dwelt alone, secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute.
Dwelling alone, secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute, they [realized] that goal for which sons of good family [leave the household life].

Having shaved off their hair and beard and donned saffron robes, they go forth from the home to the homeless life with perfect faith. Having realized for themselves through direct higher knowledge and attained in this very life that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life, they declare: "Birth is exhausted; the holy life has been lived; what was to be done has been accomplished."
"We know of no further existence beyond this.
At that time, there were sixty Arhats in the world, and the Blessed One was the sixty-first.
Section 21.

Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, I am liberated from all fetters, both divine and human; you too, monks, are liberated from all fetters, both divine and human. Wander forth, monks, on your journey for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for its benefit."
"For the welfare and happiness of gods and humans, let not two of you go by the same way. I too shall set out on a journey toward Urubilvā, to the village of Senāyanī.
Then it occurred to Māra the Evil One: "This ascetic Gautama is staying at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park."
In the Deer Park, he taught the Dharma to his disciples thus: "O monks, I am liberated from all fetters, both divine and human;

you too, O monks, are liberated from all fetters, both divine and human. Go forth, O monks, on your journey; we shall set out for the welfare of many people," and so on as before, until: "I too [shall go] to Urubilvā."
"Thinking, 'I shall set out on my journey toward the village of Senāyanagrāma,' [the Blessed One considered], 'What if I were to approach him for the purpose of causing distraction?
Then Māra, the Evil One, having transformed himself into the appearance of a young brahmin, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, at that time he spoke this verse:"
Being unliberated yet having the perception of being liberated,
why do you think, "I am liberated"?
You are bound by great fetters.
O ascetic, you shall not escape me.
Then it occurred to the Blessed One: "This is Māra, the Evil One, who has approached for the purpose of causing distraction. Having understood this, he spoke this verse:
"I am released from all fetters, both those that are divine and those that are human."
Know this, O Evil One:
you, O Death, have been defeated here.
Then it occurred to Māra, the Evil One: "The ascetic Gautama knows my mind with his own mind. Realizing this, he became sorrowful, dejected, and full of regret, and vanished right there.
Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, I am liberated from all fetters, both divine and human; you too, monks, are liberated from all fetters, both divine and human. Wander forth!"
"Monks, for the welfare of many people—as previously described—up until: 'I too shall set out on a journey toward Uruvilvā, to the village of Senāyanī.
"So be it, Venerable Sir," the monks replied to the Blessed One and departed to wander through the countryside.
